column1: G1: When is this goal done?
column2: G1 Two apps, one build. Done when Northstar's investigation and Spend Review's queue and form come through the supported authoring path on one build digest, no platform code branches on a tenant or space name, and each of the demo's eight reductions names the platform seam that replaces it (P15; §18).

column1: G2: When is this goal done?
column2: G2 Publication and saved work are governed. Done when a publication binds exact definition, input-contract, record-schema and renderer identities; Northstar's review policy and an owner-publish policy work; a stale approval or any author or model policy change is refused; pinned work adopts a version only by explicit compare-and-set (P09, P10).

column1: G3: When is this goal done?
column2: G3 Every number is exact and has a receipt. Done when the fixtures recompute (1,140,000 bytes, 900,000 unmatched; 64,000 cents), totals cover the full authorized input before pagination, windows are half-open, currency is integer cents, never mixed, every result carries a receipt pinning sources, operators and record snapshot, and a response from a stale epoch is discarded (P06).

column1: G4: When is this goal done?
column2: G4 Internal records persist, retry safely and conflict visibly. Done when a form-written record survives reload, a timeout retry with the same idempotency key yields one mutation, and two concurrent edits yield one commit and one visible conflict, never last-writer-wins, at A2's rate (P07).

column1: G5: When is this goal done?
column2: G5 Organizations cannot reach each other. Done when the canary organization replays every API call, search, file, record, job and cache lookup with Northstar's identifiers and gets nothing, and revocation reaches an open display within 5 seconds (P11).

column1: G6: When is this goal done?
column2: G6 The AI is labeled, bounded and dispensable. Done when each creation is labeled retrieval, adaptation or generation; of ten supported and five adversarial intents, every admitted result validates and every unsupported abstains; injected evidence widens nothing; in a provider outage, navigation, published queries and forms work and generation fails visibly (P12, P13).

column1: G7: When is this goal done?
column2: G7 (fuzzy) Cheaper than the spreadsheet it replaces. A team forms and keeps a second app with less effort than its spreadsheet and scripts; measurable only against a pilot baseline that does not yet exist.

column1: A1: What is assumed, and what changes if it is wrong?
column2: A1 Population. 10 organizations × 10 members = 100 seats; 3 active each = 30 concurrent. If wrong: admission, isolation and cost are reworked before a pilot.

column1: A2: What is assumed, and what changes if it is wrong?
column2: A2 Interactive load. One interaction per user per 10 s = 3/s, 18 query operations/s over six linked views, 2 submissions/s on one record. If wrong: queue controls, never weaker authorization.

column1: A3: What is assumed, and what changes if it is wrong?
column2: A3 Source volume. 20 revisions × 10 organizations × 25 MiB = 4.88 GiB of originals a month, twice that normalized, 43.95 GiB over 90 days, before records, indexes, audit and backups. If wrong: measure before costing.

column1: A4: What is assumed, and what changes if it is wrong?
column2: A4 Bounds. CSV at most 100 MiB and 1 million records; XLSX at most 10 MiB compressed, 100 MiB expanded, 10,000 rows × 32 columns per sheet; parse time and memory bounded. If wrong: reduce until demonstrated.

column1: A5: What is assumed, and what changes if it is wrong?
column2: A5 Admission. One import and one generation job per organization, three and five globally, a capped visible queue. If wrong: fair scheduling or separate workers, never silent loss.

column1: A6: What is assumed, and what changes if it is wrong?
column2: A6 Lifecycle, synthetic only. 90-day retention and audit, seven-day backups, idempotency outcomes kept 24 hours. If wrong: customer retention, deletion and retry horizon are open questions, not these values.

column1: A7: What is assumed, and what changes if it is wrong?
column2: A7 Recovery. RPO 24 hours and RTO 4 hours proven by restore; records survive a restart. If wrong: backup, replication and cost change.

column1: A8: What is assumed, and what changes if it is wrong?
column2: A8 Operating model. One managed browser offering, one region, one operator, manual membership, a named owner before live data. If wrong: region, providers, team and support hours are open; a team relaxes paging.

column1: A9: What is assumed, and what changes if it is wrong?
column2: A9 Hosting. AWS, one region (design A v4's choice) until the head rules otherwise. If wrong: section 11's hosting and cost change.

column1: A10: What is assumed, and what changes if it is wrong?
column2: A10 Generation provider. Claude behind a provider interface, re-verified at the claims phase. If wrong: the adapter swaps and the disclosure policy renames (C12).

column1: A11: What is assumed, and what changes if it is wrong?
column2: A11 Identity. fAuth (getforma-dev/gatewasm at b750ca53) is the first adapter; its viability check passed (review/fauth-viability.md); its sign-in is ruled in (2026-10-23, delegated to the lead) as a quiet real moment, a minimal platform login behind the same boundary as the fallback. If wrong: section 6's sessions change, not authority semantics.

column1: A12: What is assumed, and what changes if it is wrong?
column2: A12 Data. Synthetic only; Northstar is fictional. If wrong: data classes, threat model and policy are settled before any real row.

column1: A13: What is assumed, and what changes if it is wrong?
column2: A13 Precedence. The controlling definition governs where the two product definitions differ. If wrong: the security-first framing returns; sections 2, 3 and the demo's acts are recut.

column1: A14: What is assumed, and what changes if it is wrong?
column2: A14 Stack. FORMA-232 and FORMA-246 are done before the build ships and the review's 4.2 contracts hold at 2006423b. If wrong: the canvas route must fit 28,100 B by measurement (426 B of headroom, review 4.3); a moved contract reopens K1.

column1: A15: What is assumed, and what changes if it is wrong?
column2: A15 Peak. Every seat active at once, 3.3 times average. If wrong: admission limits and N1's node count move, not the contracts.

column1: A16: What is assumed, and what changes if it is wrong?
column2: A16 Record cadence. One record a minute per active practitioner, about 2 KiB with its audit row. If wrong: section 8's capacity and N3's commit window change.

column1: A17: What is assumed, and what changes if it is wrong?
column2: A17 Search freshness. The catalog index may lag a publication by 60 s and reauthorizes on use. If wrong: rebuild on publication; retrieval never grants access.

column1: A18: What is assumed, and what changes if it is wrong?
column2: A18 Roles. Two or three builders, one reviewer, one administrator among ten members. If wrong: section 4's rates rescale.

N1 Scalability. Ten times the design point (100 organizations, 1,000 seats, 300 concurrent on average, 600 operations/s at peak) by adding query and app capacity with no contract or code change; the design point fits one PostgreSQL and one query node. Confirmed by open-loop load at 10x on one build.

N2 Availability. No contractual figure until hosting, a support owner and failure measurements exist (A8; the definition, §13). Internal objective for the published-app path (R13): 99.5% of valid requests a month, 3.65 hours, which one full restore at RTO (A7) would exceed by 21 minutes, so the objective assumes none in a month, measured at the gateway; generation and explanation fail visibly with no objective.

N3 Latency at the client, authorization and network included, from real-user telemetry per business hour (10,800 interactions, enough for p99). SLO: median and p99 below the table in 99% of business hours a month; the targets are VALIDATION's candidates. Generation and import are cold paths: state within 1 s, duration measured, not promised. First paint: Core Web Vitals, LCP 2.5 s at p75 per device class, Forma code under 28,100 B gzip a route (27,674 B measured, review 4.3). Navigation: home, space, app open · Criticality: critical · p50: 250 ms · p99: 1 s / Warm bounded query, one six-view refresh (each operation at p99.83) · Criticality: critical · p50: 500 ms · p99: 2 s / Record commit acknowledgement, one transaction (C07) · Criticality: critical · p50: 300 ms · p99: 1 s / Revocation to an open display (the epoch poll plus one request); new requests reauthorize · Criticality: important · p99: 5 s

N4 Fault tolerance. Safety: no fault serves another organization's data, widens authority, duplicates a record or shows a number without a receipt. Liveness: queued jobs complete or fail visibly; committed records survive a restart; RPO 24 h and RTO 4 h proven by restore into an isolated environment (A7; P14).

N5 Consistency. Record commands are linearizable per record: one PostgreSQL transaction enforces idempotency, expected version, audit and membership epoch (C07; safety); publication and adoption are atomic compare-and-set (C09, C10; safety); the submitter reads their own write; search may lag 60 s and reauthorizes on use; revocation reaches open displays within 5 s (liveness) and every new request reauthorizes (safety). Confirmed by G4's retry and conflict tests and S06's two-way ordering test.

N6 Accuracy. Exact integer arithmetic, server-side, on the fixtures: 1,140,000 bytes, 900,000 unmatched, 114,000 bytes a minute over the full ten minutes; 64,000 cents and the 45,000-cent queue; no floating-point money, no cross-currency sum without a declared conversion (S02, S05). On the frozen ten supported and five adversarial intents every admitted result validates, every unsupported one abstains and every number matches its receipt (VALIDATION); fifteen is diagnostic, not a score.

N7 Security. Nothing of one organization reaches another; no model output, copied link, stale job or guessed identifier widens authority (C01, C11, C12); confirmed by the cross-tenant suite against the canary organization and the S06 table.

N8 Privacy. The composer sees schemas and synthetic examples by default; real rows reach the provider only under a policy naming the fields; raw evidence never enters prompt or audit logs (C08, C12); confirmed by inspecting every provider request in the evaluation run.

N9 Maintainability. One build runs both apps with zero commits and deploys between them, its runtime naming no tenant (P15, R14; C13); Forma pinned at v3.0.0 (2006423b) with FORMA-232 and FORMA-246 assumed done (K3).

N10 Cost. The budget is unknown (A8), so the requirement is the meter: hosts, stores, query work, model tokens, backups and egress attributed per organization monthly, generation stopped at a configured budget (C15); section 11 derives the figure.
N11 Sustainability. No separate target: model calls dominate the footprint, and retrieval before generation (R4) plus the budget stop (N10) bound them; one region (A9).

N12 Accessibility. WCAG 2.2 AA for the shell and the component library (review I-1): automatic checks on every component state at build, a keyboard-only run of S01 and a screen-reader pass per release; light or dark and other settings persist (the definition, §5).

column1: SR1: What must hold, and how is it tested?
column2: SR1 Every read and write MUST be scoped by the session's organization, DuckDB confined to its cache (M1, M2, M18, M19, M36, M37, M39). Test: the canary suite and hostile-view corpus, zero leaks, no foreign search hit, no export beyond its grant.

column1: SR2: What must hold, and how is it tested?
column2: SR2 One adapter MUST verify fAuth's token offline behind back-channel PKCE, re-check the epoch per request, refuse cross-site changes (M3 to M7, M24, M25, M45). Test: forged token, reused code, revoked cookie, cross-site POST refused within 5 s.

column1: SR3: What must hold, and how is it tested?
column2: SR3 Internal calls MUST carry a signed service token the callee re-checks; roles hold disjoint grants (M16, M17). Test: workspace cannot insert a publication.

column1: SR4: What must hold, and how is it tested?
column2: SR4 The model MUST reach only five tools, none returning rows, and read untrusted text as data; proposals validated whole (M26, M27, M30, M31). Test: the fifteen-intent suite, S06's injected field, no query result in any provider request.

column1: SR5: What must hold, and how is it tested?
column2: SR5 Imports MUST parse in a WebAssembly sandbox with no system interface, under A4's caps (M8, M9). Test: an XLSX inflating past 100 MiB refused; fuzzing; a module importing a socket or file interface rejected at build.

column1: SR6: What must hold, and how is it tested?
column2: SR6 Publication MUST check digest, policy version and approver epoch in one SERIALIZABLE transaction, approver ≠ author (M10, M11). Test: stale, replayed approvals refused.

column1: SR7: What must hold, and how is it tested?
column2: SR7 Results MUST be re-authorized before release and match their receipt; idempotency keys scoped to organization, principal, work and command (M20, M21, M32, M33, M40, M44, M46, M47). Test: canary digest denied; another principal's key finds nothing; re-derivation matches.

column1: SR8: What must hold, and how is it tested?
column2: SR8 Releases MUST build from pinned lockfiles and SHA-pinned actions, signed, with an SBOM (M12, M13). Inspection: provenance; an unsigned digest refused.

column1: SR9: What must hold, and how is it tested?
column2: SR9 Operator access MUST be just in time, breakglass sealed with an outside reader, destructive changes two-person, an organization's deletion after a 24-hour hold (M14, M15, M49). Demonstration: both drills.

column1: SR10: What must hold, and how is it tested?
column2: SR10 Audit MUST be insert-only, hash-chained and anchored every 15 minutes (M22, M23). Test: no role updates or deletes; chain verified.

column1: SR11: What must hold, and how is it tested?
column2: SR11 Data MUST be minimised and shredded: per-organization keys, policy-named fields only, allowlisted logs, tombstones replayed after restore (M34, M35, M38, M41 to M43, M48). Test: restore drill, provider-request inspection, log scan.

column1: SR13: What must hold, and how is it tested?
column2: SR13 Definition strings MUST render escaped and SVG MUST be built from numbers, never strings (M50, M51). Test: the hostile-definition corpus; no CSP report.

column1: SR12: What must hold, and how is it tested?
column2: SR12 Every security control MUST fail closed and every organization MUST stay inside its slots and budget (M28, M29). Test: unreachable key set, KMS or membership refuses; 10x load spares others.

column1: SI1: What must always hold, and which component enforces it?
column2: SI1 (safety) Scope: every read and write is scoped by the verified session's organization, never a request value. Enforcers: the session adapter, the organization's only source; the authorizer; row-level security; per-organization prefixes and key policies (D3).

column1: SI2: What must always hold, and which component enforces it?
column2: SI2 (safety) Authority: no model output, file, link or stale job widens authority; the model proposes data (D1). Enforcers: P5's validation, P3's admission, the authorizer, the sandbox runtime, the view server's typed props and escaping, which pass no markup (M50).

column1: SI3: What must always hold, and which component enforces it?
column2: SI3 (safety) Governed writes: members see only publications control wrote under policy over an approved digest; a record changes only by a declared command, once per key, under the current epoch. Enforcers: the publisher's SERIALIZABLE transaction, the record store's locked transaction (D2, D5), the roles' grants.

column1: SI4: What must always hold, and which component enforces it?
column2: SI4 (liveness) Revocation: a removed membership or grant stops new results within 5 s and queued ones at execution and delivery. Enforcers: the authorizer's epoch read, P4's re-checks (F34), the canvas's 5 s epoch poll.

column1: SI5: What must always hold, and which component enforces it?
column2: SI5 (safety) Audit: every governance action, operator access and record command is an append-only row no role updates or deletes. Enforcers: the audit table's row policies, insert-only grants, 10.6's anchors.

column1: SI6: What must always hold, and which component enforces it?
column2: SI6 (liveness) Fair share: one organization's load never takes another below N2 or N3. Enforcers: the edge's limits, per-organization query and job slots, the budget stop (N10).

column1: D1: What was decided, which door is it, and what does it serve?
column2: Decision: A typed AppDefinition (C04): views over a closed vocabulary, a bounded query grammar, record schemas and declared commands, interpreted by first-party renderers; the model proposes data, never code, markup or grants (K1; design A D13 reversed) · Door: one-way: every stored app is in it · Serves: N9, N7, G1, G6 · Cost: complexity: a new primitive is a release · Alternatives: markup on Forma 3.1; both (12.2) · Section: 6, 8 · Binds demo: yes · D1, the representation. Drivers: N7, G6, G1, N9, N3's 28,100 B, the critical path. (A) Design A's D13, model-written HTML on Forma 3.1's HTML runtime: optimises for expressiveness; needs FORMA-237 to 242 (five P1 tickets, two security-critical), keeps two High/High threat rows (as-built TH11, TH22) and loads a 28,337 B gzip runtime against the 28,100 B route budget (review 4.3); loses against N7, N9 and the critical path. (B) Both representations at once: optimises for each app's best fit; doubles what a reviewer approves; loses against G2 and N7. (Chosen) a typed AppDefinition (C04) interpreted by first-party compiled renderers. Chosen because the controlling definition describes it (§9: "new working behavior"; §15: no arbitrary untrusted module), the review's experiment rendered a four-kind canvas on 3.0.0 as shipped (review 4.3), and two apps through one path (§18) is a proof a closed vocabulary makes structural. …

column1: D2: What was decided, which door is it, and what does it serve?
column2: Decision: An atomic publication record the control plane alone writes, binding exact definition, input contracts, record schemas and renderer versions under the organization's versioned policy; the reviewer's own session approves the content digest (C09; design A D15) · Door: one-way: the organization's evidence · Serves: G2, N7, R9 · Cost: operations · Alternatives: approval in the editor; step-up required (12.2) · Section: 6, 7 · Binds demo: yes; owner publication under its low-risk policy · D2, the publication record. Drivers: G2, R9, N5. (L) Publication by the workspace server under the author's session: optimises for one fewer role; lets the role that handles model output publish; loses against G2 and N7. (M) A signed manifest without a record: optimises for fewer parts; gives adoption (D14) nothing to compare-and-set against; loses against N5 and R10. (N) Design A's D15, a WebAuthn assertion on every approval: optimises for non-repudiation; forbids the owner-publish policy R9 requires; loses against G2. (Chosen) the atomic record of 5.3, written by the control plane alone, approved by the reviewer's own session over the content digest, step-up a policy option. Chosen because the writer of publications must not handle model output. Good: a small trusted core. Bad: one more role. Confirmed by SR3's test and G2's stale-approval refusal.

column1: D3: What was decided, which door is it, and what does it serve?
column2: Decision: Pooled tenancy: organization id in every key, row-level security, one data key per organization; cells later (C01; design A D16) · Door: one-way: ids added later migrate every store · Serves: N7, N1, G5 · Cost: security surface · Alternatives: a silo per tenant (12.2) · Section: 8, 10 · Binds demo: yes, from the first row · D3, pooled tenancy. Drivers: N7, G5, A8, N10. (J) A silo, a database and key per organization: optimises for isolation by construction; ten databases now, a hundred at N1, run alone; loses against A8 and N10. A schema per organization: optimises for export; shares roles and multiplies migrations; loses against N9. (Chosen) pooled rows, the organization id in every key, row-level security, one data key per organization, cells later (C01). Chosen because the pool has two independent walls: against a query omitting its organization, the id from the verified token and the row policy; against a role setting the wrong id, the adapter as the id's only source (R15) and the canary suite (G5). Good: one schema to migrate. Bad: a policy bug is a cross-organization bug, so the suite runs every release. Confirmed by that suite and by moving one synthetic organization to a cell in a drill.

column1: D4: What was decided, which door is it, and what does it serve?
column2: Decision: Immutable Parquet revisions queried by DuckDB through typed queries for sources; PostgreSQL for records, work and publications; one data service owns both behind receipts and commands (K5; design A D19) · Door: one-way: what receipts and work are made of · Serves: G3, N6, N3, N5 · Cost: complexity: two stores, two engines · Alternatives: PostgreSQL tables per dataset; SQLite per revision (12.2) · Section: 8 · Binds demo: yes · D4, sources and records. Drivers: G3, N3's 2 s six-view refresh over 1 million records, G4, N6. (D) PostgreSQL tables per dataset: optimises for one store already run; puts millions of rows a revision in the database every role uses; loses against N3 and N9. (E) SQLite per revision: optimises for an embedded engine; reads whole rows for a two-column aggregate; loses against N3. Records in Parquet too: optimises for one engine; gives a form no transaction; loses against G4 and N5. (Chosen) immutable Parquet revisions queried by DuckDB through the typed grammar; records, work and publications in PostgreSQL; one data service behind receipts (C06) and commands (C07). Chosen because evidence never changes and records always do. Good: receipts pin a revision forever; a command is one transaction. Bad: two engines; an unmeasured cold aggregate. …

column1: D5: What was decided, which door is it, and what does it serve?
column2: Decision: Record commands: idempotency outcome first, then expected version, membership epoch and work and app revision in one PostgreSQL transaction; a conflict returns an authorized recovery view (C07) · Door: two-way at the protocol · Serves: G4, N5, N4 · Cost: complexity · Alternatives: last-writer-wins (12.2) · Section: 7, 9 · Binds demo: yes

column1: D6: What was decided, which door is it, and what does it serve?
column2: Decision: One identity adapter with one verified-principal check; fAuth first, organization from tenant_id, membership and roles the platform's own (K4; design A D18) · Door: two-way at the protocol · Serves: R15, N7 · Cost: complexity · Alternatives: a commercial identity provider (12.2) · Section: 6, 10 · Binds demo: the token contract yes; the provider no

column1: D7: What was decided, which door is it, and what does it serve?
column2: Decision: Retrieval over catalog metadata and curated examples, embedded in process, per-organization index files built by workers; a hit is re-checked for authorization and compatibility (C03; design A D20) · Door: two-way: derived · Serves: R4, N7, N10 · Cost: money · Alternatives: a hosted vector database (12.2) · Section: 6 · Binds demo: the interface yes

column1: D8: What was decided, which door is it, and what does it serve?
column2: Decision: Generation and explanation as jobs behind a provider interface on schemas and synthetic rows; whole-output validation; at most two attempts; visible job state (C08, C12; design A D21) · Door: two-way · Serves: G6, N8, R13, N10 · Cost: money, operations · Alternatives: generation inside the request (12.2) · Section: 6, 7 · Binds demo: yes, not the provider

column1: D9: What was decided, which door is it, and what does it serve?
column2: Decision: Edits as patches on a base revision with a semantic diff; undo is a revision; definition revisions never touch committed records (C08; design A D22) · Door: two-way · Serves: R5, R10 · Cost: complexity · Alternatives: edits in memory (12.2) · Section: 6 · Binds demo: yes

column1: D10: What was decided, which door is it, and what does it serve?
column2: Decision: One native canvas island over resolved presentation props: boolean kind flags, nested lists, SVG built server-side from numbers; geometry and keyboard code ported from genui-runtime; linked filters re-query the server (design A D23, D40) · Door: two-way · Serves: N3, R7, N12 · Cost: complexity: 426 B of route headroom · Alternatives: a renderer per surface (12.2) · Section: 6 · Binds demo: yes

column1: D11: What was decided, which door is it, and what does it serve?
column2: Decision: One binary, roles as deployments with their own credentials; one process for the demo (design A D17) · Door: two-way · Serves: N9, R14, N2 · Cost: operations · Alternatives: a service per concern (12.2) · Section: 6, 11 · Binds demo: yes: the interfaces

column1: D12: What was decided, which door is it, and what does it serve?
column2: Decision: Connected sources read-only; internal records writable through declared commands; no external action (C14; design A D26) · Door: two-way: a new operation type · Serves: N7, R8, G4 · Cost: security surface · Alternatives: one bounded external action (12.2) · Section: 6, 10 · Binds demo: yes

column1: D13: What was decided, which door is it, and what does it serve?
column2: Decision: Assistant tools: compose, set parameters, query, explain, propose a command; the user submits every mutation; no publish or policy tool (C12; design A D39 narrowed) · Door: two-way · Serves: G6, R12, N7 · Cost: security surface · Alternatives: an agent that submits (12.2) · Section: 6, 9, 10 · Binds demo: yes

column1: D14: What was decided, which door is it, and what does it serve?
column2: Decision: Saved work pins its publication; adoption is explicit compare-and-set; rollback reverses no record (C10) · Door: two-way · Serves: G2, R10, N5 · Cost: complexity · Alternatives: automatic upgrade (12.2) · Section: 7, 8 · Binds demo: yes

column1: D15: What was decided, which door is it, and what does it serve?
column2: Decision: AWS, one region: ECS on Fargate, RDS Multi-AZ, S3, KMS, CloudFront, ALB, WAF (A9; design A D27) · Door: two-way; one-way per organization once its data lives there · Serves: N2, N4, N10 · Cost: money · Alternatives: Kubernetes; provider-neutral hosting (12.2) · Section: 11 · Binds demo: no: the demo runs on one host

column1: TH1: What is the threat, and the response?
column2: Elements and boundaries crossed: B7, P2, P4, DS1, DS2, F27, F31 · STRIDE: Information disclosure; Elevation of privilege · Threat statement: A member of any organization (TA2, TA3) with a guessed or copied identifier, or a handler omitting its scope, can read or act on Northstar's work, records, revisions or receipts, which leads to one organization's data served to another, negatively impacting AS3, AS4 · Invariant: SI1 · Existing control: tenant_id in fAuth's token [built]; the platform ignores the slug header, which fAuth itself honours as a fallback · Response and mitigation: mitigate. M1 prevent: the organization from the session only; row-level security on every table; keys under o/{org}/; KMS encryption contexts the key policy requires; per-query S3 sessions scoped to the prefix. M2 detect: the canary's cross-tenant suite each release (G5); cross-organization identifiers audited, 10 an hour alert · Likelihood/impact; status; residual: High/High; proposed; Low

column1: TH2: What is the threat, and the response?
column2: Elements and boundaries crossed: B8, EE3, DS5, F23, F24, F25 · STRIDE: Spoofing · Threat statement: Whoever holds fAuth's signing or management key (TA1, TA9) can mint a token for any sub and tenant_id or create a user anywhere, which leads to a session as any member, negatively impacting AS1 · Invariant: SI1, SI2 · Existing control: EdDSA tokens with kid; one key in the key set; invite-only tenants [built] · Response and mitigation: mitigate; transfer custody to fAuth (the head). M3 prevent: a session only for an invited sub, so a forged unknown sub gets nothing; R15's checks, an unknown kid refetched once a minute, then refused. M4 detect: mints audited with kid and iat; an unknown kid alerts. M5, fAuth's: the key unexportable in KMS, current and next published (FORMA-248) · Likelihood/impact; status; residual: Low/High; M3, M4 proposed; M5 deferred; Medium: AR4 until M5 lands

column1: TH3: What is the threat, and the response?
column2: Elements and boundaries crossed: B1, B8, EE1, EE3, P2, F22, F23 · STRIDE: Spoofing; Tampering · Threat statement: An outside attacker (TA1) with a lure link can sign the victim's browser in as the attacker, or replay a code or token from the handoff, which leads to the victim's evidence in the attacker's organization or a stolen session, negatively impacting AS1, AS4 · Invariant: SI1 · Existing control: fAuth's hosted page with PKCE S256; a SameSite=None refresh cookie on its origin [built] · Response and mitigation: mitigate. M6 prevent: a registered client completing the authorization-code flow with PKCE S256 on the back channel, state bound to a 10-minute pre-session cookie, no token in browser script, the refresh-cookie bridge unused; the shell names organization and person on every page. M7 detect: callback refusals audited; 5 in 10 minutes from one address alert · Likelihood/impact; status; residual: Medium/High; proposed; Low

column1: TH4: What is the threat, and the response?
column2: Elements and boundaries crossed: B6, P6, DS2, F6, F7, F8, F9 · STRIDE: Denial of service; Elevation of privilege · Threat statement: A builder (TA3), or whoever hands them a file, can drop a bomb (a 9 MiB XLSX inflating past 100 MiB) or a parser exploit, which leads to a worker exhausted or code running beside the provider key and every organization's revisions, negatively impacting AS4, AS5 · Invariant: SI2, SI6 · Existing control: none; the prototypes' browser cap (section 2) is not this system's · Response and mitigation: mitigate. M8 prevent: P6 a WebAssembly module with no system interface beyond two streams, so no socket and no credentials endpoint; A4's caps, 2 GiB and 120 s of fuel, enforced by the runtime; the worker alone uploads; no macro, formula or link engine. M9 detect: a killed or crashed sandbox audited with its reason, two an hour from one organization alert; both parsers fuzzed in CI · Likelihood/impact; status; residual: High/High; proposed; Low

column1: TH5: What is the threat, and the response?
column2: Elements and boundaries crossed: B3, P3, DS1, F15, F16, F17 · STRIDE: Tampering; Repudiation · Threat statement: A builder (TA3) patching after approval, or anyone replaying an approval after the reviewer's revocation, can publish content the reviewer never saw and can deny, which leads to a publication nobody approved, negatively impacting AS2, AS7 · Invariant: SI3, SI5 · Existing control: none · Response and mitigation: mitigate. M10 prevent: an approval is the reviewer's own session over the admitted digest; the publisher's SERIALIZABLE transaction checks it against the draft's current digest, the policy version and the approver's epoch, under a CHECK that approver ≠ author unless owner publication; the inbox renders the admitted bytes; an approval is spent by publication or voided by the next patch. M11 detect: mismatched or replayed approvals audited; 3 an hour alert · Likelihood/impact; status; residual: High/High; proposed; Low

column1: TH6: What is the threat, and the response?
column2: Elements and boundaries crossed: B2, P1 to P8, DS1 · STRIDE: Tampering · Threat statement: A hostile crate, npm package, action or DuckDB release (TA7), or a compromised workflow (TA8), can ship code in a release every role runs (SA1), which leads to every organization compromised at once, negatively impacting every asset · Invariant: SI1 to SI6 · Existing control: Forma's crates pin each other at =3.0.0; the walker is fuzzed (forma SECURITY.md) [built] · Response and mitigation: mitigate. M12 prevent: Forma at v3.0.0 = 2006423b, every crate and npm package pinned by lockfile and checksum; advisory and licence checks in CI; actions pinned to commit SHAs; the release built from a tag only the head may create, its image digest signed by OIDC-federated keyless signing, a CycloneDX SBOM beside it under Object Lock, deployed by digest only; the coding agent's identity cannot tag, edit workflows or merge. M13 detect: deployed SBOMs scanned daily; a change to admission, the permission table or a workflow alerts · Likelihood/impact; status; residual: Low/High; proposed; Medium: AR8

column1: TH7: What is the threat, and the response?
column2: Elements and boundaries crossed: EE2, P2, DS1, DS3, F2, F3 · STRIDE: Elevation of privilege; Information disclosure; Repudiation · Threat statement: The operator (TA9), or whoever holds their credentials, can read an organization's data, delete it, or alter the record of doing so, which leads to Confidential data read or destroyed outside the organization's governance, negatively impacting AS3, AS4, AS5, AS7 · Invariant: SI1, SI5 · Existing control: none · Response and mitigation: mitigate; accept the one-person case (AR1). M14 prevent: the operator role sees no organization data (R16); reading it needs a just-in-time grant the administrator approves, one hour under that key; breakglass is a sealed IAM role behind a hardware key whose CloudTrail a named outside reviewer reads; deletion, key disablement, mass sign-out and permission-table changes take two people (10.5). M15 detect: breakglass alerts the reviewer first; a just-in-time session alerts the administrators; CloudTrail reviewed monthly · Likelihood/impact; status; residual: Low/High; proposed; Medium: AR1, AR9

column1: AR1: What risk was accepted, and why?
column2: Accepted risk: One operator: platform-wide destructive actions wait 24 hours with notice instead of a second person; the operator role self-granted with a reason · Reason: one founder (A8); operator pages share the member plane under the operator role; until a named outside reader exists, breakglass alerts the head alone

column1: AR2: What risk was accepted, and why?
column2: Accepted risk: Pooled roles: a compromised workspace reads what any member may read, a compromised data service every revision · Reason: a silo is ten stacks for one operator (12.2); per-organization keys and the canary suite bound it

column1: AR3: What risk was accepted, and why?
column2: Accepted risk: Plaintext HTTP inside the VPC, ALB to tasks and role to role · Reason: mTLS needs a certificate authority nobody runs (A8); SA1 makes a compromised task fatal anyway

column1: AR4: What risk was accepted, and why?
column2: Accepted risk: fAuth's signing and management keys sit with the same founder on one deployment; a compromise mints any invited principal (M3) · Reason: FORMA-248 moves the key into KMS before any real organization

column1: AR5: What risk was accepted, and why?
column2: Accepted risk: A worker that dies after its provider call pays twice · Reason: the lease's cost against a store for request ids

column1: AR6: What risk was accepted, and why?
column2: Accepted risk: A disabled KMS key may serve an already-unwrapped data key until the key is next used, with no vendor time bound · Reason: the tombstone and epoch stop reads in our code first

column1: AR7: What risk was accepted, and why?
column2: Accepted risk: The provider retains what a policy lets through, under its terms · Reason: the organization's administrator chooses policy and provider (N8)

column1: AR8: What risk was accepted, and why?

column1: The summary says D15's region door closes per organization. Before reading 5.3, predict what an organization that wants to move to another region a year in would have to move, and what it could leave behind. Then, when you reach 10.7, find the accepted risk that says why its backups do not shorten the list.
column2: Everything made of the four one-way doors: its originals and Parquet revisions under its key, its PostgreSQL rows (records, work, publications, audit), the key itself, and the receipts that pin all of them; derived data (index files, caches, previews) can be left and rebuilt. Its backups stay in the region (AR10 in 10.7), so they are part of what moves, not a shortcut (1, 5.3, 8, 10.7).

column1: Suppose Maya's sheet had shown 228,000 with the label "bytes per minute over the observed events". The number is now honestly labelled. Argue which of section 2's six failures that label removes and which remain, then say what the design does that a well-labelled sheet cannot.
column2: It removes only the missing denominator in step 3, and only for a reader who notices the label. Steps 1, 2, 4, 5 and 6 remain: no source revision, a match rule in Maya's head, rows leaving the company, a verdict without its window and inventory revision, and an overwritable cell. The design binds the denominator into the definition (a 10-minute window) and the receipt pins it with the revisions and the rule, so a later reader cannot get 228,000 from the same app (2, R6, G3).

column1: A3 budgets the normalized copy at twice the originals. Predict which direction A3's 43.95 GiB moves if the spike measures Parquet revisions smaller than their CSV originals, say why the record budgets high anyway, and name the two numbers in section 11 that would shrink with it.
column2: Down: the 29.3 GiB of Parquet is two thirds of the total, so a Parquet copy at the original's size would bring the 90-day figure to about 29.3 GiB. The record budgets twice "until measured" because only measured numbers are facts and an over-estimate errs toward spare disk. The data tasks' 50 GiB disk in 11.2 and the S3 line (60 GiB) would shrink (A3, 8, 11.2).

column1: A15's peak factor of 3.3 assumes every seat active at once. Rebuild the design point at a peak of 2 times average instead, carry it into 5.2's in-flight number and N1's 10x row, and say which numbers do not move.
column2: 18 operations a second times 2 is 36 at peak; at 100 ms that is 3.6 in flight, well inside one node's 8 slots; at 10x, 360 a second is 36 in flight, five data tasks plus one for a zone loss instead of eight plus one. The per-organization cap of 2, the p99.83 per operation, the contracts and every safety property do not move, which is exactly what A15's "if wrong" clause says (4.2, A15, 5.2, 11.2).

column1: Little's law gives 6 in flight at 100 ms. Suppose the spike measures a warm operation at 200 ms. Recompute, and say what breaks at the design point and what still holds.
column2: 60 a second times 0.2 s is 12 in flight, above the node's 8 slots, so the design point no longer fits one node and operations queue (429 past 20 waiting an organization). The per-organization cap of 2 makes a six-view refresh three waves of 200 ms, about 600 ms warm, still inside N3's 2 s, and nothing about isolation or receipts changes. Section 13.2's "a third task and a cap of 6" is the record's own prepared answer (5.2, 6.3, 13.2).

column1: D4 is a one-way door and DuckDB is not, though DuckDB is the engine that reads D4's Parquet. Explain the difference, using what a receipt pins.
column2: A receipt pins revision digests, operator versions, parameters and a record snapshot, never an engine or a plan. Swapping DuckDB, or precomputing aggregates at admission, changes how a result is produced, and the re-derivation must still match; the Parquet layout and the PostgreSQL rows are what every receipt and every case is made of, so changing them migrates every organization (D4, 6.3, 12.2's D4 record).

column1: A colleague proposes caching the membership row for 30 s in the workspace server to save the 60 reads a second at peak. Name the requirement row the change breaks and the property the record pays for instead, and say what the proof of that property becomes with the cache.
column2: N3's revocation row: an open display denied within 5 s, and "revocation proved by a read". With a 30 s cache a removed member keeps reading for up to 30 s and the proof becomes a staleness bound you argue about instead of a read you can test. The record spends two primary reads a request, 120 a second at peak, to keep it a read; section 10.2 later names the property as the fourth invariant (6.1, N3, 8).

column1: Make the case, in two sentences, for letting the workspace server write the publication under the author's session (alternative L), then say what the record protects by refusing it.
column2: For: one fewer role to run, and one fewer hop on the publish path for a founder who runs everything alone. Against: the workspace server is the role that handles the member's request and forwards model output, so a flaw there could insert a publication nobody approved; D2 keeps the only publication writer one database grant away from model output, and SR3's test proves workspace cannot insert one (6.2, D2, 12.2).

column1: Swap the first two steps of the record command: check the expected version before looking up the idempotency outcome. Trace the lost-response retry of ik-1 and say what the member sees.
column2: The first attempt committed version 1. The retry carries expected version 0; a version check first finds version 1 and returns 409 with a recovery view, so the member believes the decision failed and may submit it again under a new key, producing a second mutation or a confusing conflict. Outcome first finds ik-1 and returns the original outcome, one mutation (6.3, 7.3 messages 9 to 14, 9).

column1: Predict what a successful exploit of the XLSX parser can reach in this design, then what it could reach if the parser ran as ordinary code inside the worker process.
column2: In the sandbox: one job's bytes and two streams; no socket, file or credentials endpoint, so the job fails visibly and nothing else is touched. In the worker process: the provider key, the ability to upload under any organization's key, and every revision the worker reads; 10.4 rates that row High on both scales before the sandbox (6.4, SR5).

column1: The provider returns a proposal with seven views that all parse and an eighth whose kind, "heatmap", no renderer is registered for. Predict what is stored, what Maya sees and what the slot does. Then change it: the eighth view is valid but the proposal has 25 views.
column2: Both are refused whole. Admission checks every kind against a registered renderer and names the first check that failed; an unknown kind fails and nothing falls back, so no partial seven-view app exists, the draft is not admitted and the generation slot frees. Twenty-five views fails the complexity limit (at most 24) the same way. Maya sees the refusal with its reason, and R4 says the composer names the missing capability rather than inventing one (7.1 step 4, 6.2, R4, A5).

column1: Jordan downloads an export at 10:05; at 10:06 the administrator removes his grant while his canvas is open and one of his queries is still queued. Predict what the platform does about each of the three, and name the sentence in R11 that keeps the first honest.
column2: The export is gone: delivered data is stated as unrecallable, and the record says so rather than pretending to a remote wipe. The canvas is denied within 5 s, because it polls the epoch every 5 s and every request reauthorizes. The queued query is re-checked at execution and again before release and returns denied, nothing cached or shown; R11's "revocation stops future results, queued ones included" is the rule, and "delivered data is stated as unrecallable" is the honest half (7.2, R11, 6.5).

column1: Two practitioners submit needs_context on EXP-002 at the same instant, both with expected version 0, with keys ik-1 and ik-9. Walk the transaction for each in 6.3's lock order and say what each sees. Then say what changes if both had sent the key ik-1.
column2: Both insert their outcome rows (different keys, no clash); both take the record row FOR UPDATE; one wins, finds the record absent, commits version 1. The other waits on the row lock, then finds version 1 where it expected 0 and returns 409 with the recovery view: one commit, one visible conflict, never last-writer-wins. With the same key, nothing changes between two principals, because the key is scoped to the principal; for one principal retrying, the second insert waits on the outcome row and returns the stored outcome, one mutation (7.3, 6.3, 9).

column1: A result cache keyed by (view, parameters) alone would be fast and simple. Name the two guarantees from section 4 it breaks, give one concrete wrong answer it would serve, and say what the record keys the cache by instead.
column2: N7 (nothing of one organization reaches another): the canary with the same view and parameters would receive Northstar's total. And N3's and N5's revocation bound: a result computed for Jordan before his grant was removed would be served after it. The key is the receipt digest, which carries the organization, revisions, record sequence, parameters and policy epoch, and a hit is still re-authorized before release; 10.2 later names the two properties as its first and fourth invariants (8, 6.3, N7, N5).

column1: Argue for returning 403 rather than 404 to a member of another organization who opens Northstar's work id (it is more honest, and clients can show a better message). Then say what property of the error model it would give up, and why the one 403 the record does return is safe.
column2: A 403 tells the caller the id exists and belongs to someone, which is a one-bit leak per guess and, across many guesses, a map of another organization's work; the record's rule is that denied, foreign and absent are indistinguishable. The author's own-approval 403 is safe because she already sees the app, so no existence is revealed, and naming the rule tells her what to do (9, R11, 7.3's canary case).

column1: The island drops any page whose epoch is behind, and polls the membership epoch every 5 s, yet it is excluded from the trusted computing base. Argue why that is correct.
column2: The island runs on the member's machine, where TA3 already holds everything it holds, so nothing it enforces can be relied on. The server re-checks membership at execution and before release, and a query carries its epoch so the server, not the island, can refuse a stale one; the island's discard improves what the member sees, it does not decide what they may see (10.2, SI4, 7.2).

column1: Rewrite TH5 for a design where an approval is "approve draft 7" with no digest. Which prevent control vanishes, what sequence does the attacker run, and which of the remaining controls still holds?
column2: M10's digest binding vanishes. Maya asks Sarah to approve draft 7, Sarah approves, Maya patches the denominator into revision 8, and the publisher publishes "draft 7's current content", which Sarah never saw. The CHECK that approver is not author still holds, and so does the epoch check, but neither is about content; G2's "a stale approval is refused" becomes impossible to test (TH5, 6.2, G2).

column1: A service token minted by the workspace server for Maya at epoch 7, callee the data service, is captured inside the VPC at 10:00:00. List what an attacker can do with it and until when, then what they cannot do and which fact stops each attempt.
column2: They can call the data service as Maya, within her organization and her permissions, until 10:05:00, which is what AR3 accepts. They cannot call the control plane (the token names its callee), publish or change policy (the data service holds no such grant), act after an administrator revokes Maya (the callee re-reads the membership row), or act after 10:05 (expiry); and a replaced task rotates the signing keys (10.5, SR3, AR3, 10.6).

column1: AR2 accepts that a compromised data service can read every organization's revisions. Design the control that would remove AR2, cost it against A8 and N10, and say whether the per-organization keys already limit the exposure.
column2: The control is a data task (or a whole cell, or a silo) per organization, so one credential unwraps one key. The cost is what D3's record names: ten stacks now and a hundred at N1 for one operator, and a second data task per organization in a cost table already dominated by the data service. The keys do not limit it, because the data service's role legitimately unwraps every organization's key with its context; what bounds AR2 is detection, the canary suite each release, and the escape hatch, moving one organization to a cell when it matters (AR2, D3, 11.2, 12.2).

column1: Wave one of a release doubles the six-view refresh's p99 from 400 ms to 900 ms, with no errors and no receipt mismatches. Using only 11.1, say whether the wave rolls back and what else in 11.1 can stop a release, then explain why the rollback metric was made that narrow.
column2: No: forma_canary_failures_total alone rolls a wave back, and it counts errors, cross-tenant hits and receipt mismatches, not latency. 11.1's other brake is "any page of 11.3 blocks the next wave", and 900 ms is inside N3's 2 s, so no page fires; the regression is caught over the month by the refresh objective's budget. The metric is isolation and correctness because those are the failures a rollback must never wait on a human for; latency has budgets and pages (11.1, N3, 11.3).

column1: Rebuild the Fargate line from the sizes and unit prices, with disk at $0.000111 per GiB-hour and only the data tasks carrying the 50 GiB of disk the record sizes, then the data service's share, then the number of data tasks at 10x.
column2: 13 vCPU × 730 h × $0.04048 is about $384 and 54 GiB × 730 × $0.004445 about $175, together $559; two data tasks × 50 GiB × 730 × $0.000111 add about $8, so about $565. The data service's two tasks are 8 vCPU and 32 GiB, about $236 plus $104, the "$340" the record names, plus their disk. At 10x, 600 a second × 0.1 s is 60 in flight, at 8 a node eight tasks, plus one for a zone loss (11.2, 5.2).

column1: AL6, the oldest queued job over 10 minutes, is a ticket; AL11, an audit or anchor write failure, is a page. Argue the split from the properties each protects.
column2: A late job is a liveness delay on a cold path the member already sees as queued within 1 s; nothing is wrong about what they see, so it can wait for morning. A failed audit write means actions are happening without the append-only record SI5 promises, a safety property, and the longer it runs the larger the gap; that is worth waking someone (11.3, SI5, N3).

column1: Option B under D1, both representations at once, is dismissed in one sentence. Make its best case for the demo, then show which of G2's done-when clauses it strains and why the deferred custom-widget tier is not the same thing as B.
column2: For B: the generation moment could show a bespoke widget where the typed vocabulary shows assembly (RK6), and an app could use the best fit per view. G2 requires a publication to bind exact definition and renderer identities and a reviewer to approve exactly what runs; with two representations the reviewer approves two kinds of artifact through two admission paths, one of them needing a sanitizer, which is what "doubles what a reviewer approves" means, and N7 pays for the second path. The custom-widget tier is the markup path deferred behind its own tickets and its own threat model, not a second path in this release's approval flow (12.2, D1, G2, 3.2).

column1: RK5, the unmeasured cold aggregate, is Medium. Argue for High, then say why the record's rank holds.
column2: For High: the six-view refresh at 2 s is N3's critical row and a miss touches every published app. The rank holds because the fallback, aggregates computed at admission, changes DuckDB's plan and not the grammar, the receipts or D4, so no one-way door and no isolation property is at stake, which is 13.1's definition of High (13.1, 12.2's D4 record, 5.2).

column1: The two 99.9% factors for the platform's own roles are the record's assumption, not a vendor figure. Argue whether two tasks in two zones justify it and what measurement would replace it; then compose the warm and cold chains from appendix C's hard rows and say why one full restore does not fit N2's month.
column2: Two tasks in two zones means a zone loss or one task's crash leaves a task sized to carry the design point, so the figure assumes the remaining failures are deploys and bugs; only the failure-mode drills and a quarter of real-user availability data can replace it. Warm: 0.999 (CloudFront) × 0.9995 (RDS) × 0.999 (workspace) × 0.999 (data) is about 0.9965; cold adds S3 at 0.999 and KMS at 0.99999, about 0.9955. 99.5% of 730 hours allows 3.65 hours, 219 minutes; a 4-hour restore is 240, 21 minutes over, so N2 assumes no full restore in a month (C, 5.2, N2, 11.4).
